# Advanced methods

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## When the methods so far run out {.smaller}

Everything today assumed we could write down the likelihood and evaluate it quickly. That stops being true when

- the model is stochastic, so the same parameters give a different epidemic every run
- the state of the system (how many are infected right now) is itself unknown and has to be estimated along with the parameters
- the model is expensive enough that even MCMC's thousands of evaluations are too many
- estimates are needed as the outbreak unfolds, updated every time new data arrive

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Three families

1.  Bayesian inference with MCMC, which we have just done
2.  Particle filtering, for stochastic models where the state is hidden
3.  Approximate Bayesian computation, for when the likelihood cannot be written down at all

And, cutting across all of them, ensembles: combining several models or several fits rather than betting on one

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Particle filtering {.smaller}

A particle filter runs the stochastic model forward as a cloud of simulations, the *particles*. Each time a new data point arrives, the particles that agree with it are kept and multiplied, and the ones that do not are dropped. The surviving cloud is the distribution of the hidden state given the data so far

It is the tool of choice when

- the model is stochastic and the noise in transmission matters
- you need the current state, not just the parameters
- parameters change over time, or data go missing for a while
- the answer has to be updated in real time

Put a particle filter inside an MCMC loop and you have particle MCMC, which estimates the parameters of a stochastic model properly

## Approximate Bayesian computation {.smaller}

If you can simulate from the model but cannot write its likelihood, ABC still gets you a posterior:

1.  Draw parameters from the prior
2.  Simulate an outbreak with them
3.  Compare the simulated outbreak with the real one, usually through a few summary statistics
4.  Keep the parameters if the two are close enough, throw them away otherwise

The kept parameters are draws from an approximate posterior. The approximation is only as good as the summaries and the threshold, and the method spends most of its simulations on parameters it then rejects, but it works for models nothing else can touch

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Ensembles {.smaller}

Rather than choosing one model, one method or one dataset and standing behind it:

- average the predictions of several models
- combine estimates from least squares, MLE and MCMC
- refit the same model to resampled versions of the data, the bootstrap

The spread across the ensemble is a measure of the uncertainty that comes from those choices, which none of the individual fits can show you, and averaged predictions tend to overfit less than any single member
